transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

I’m here because… I don’t really know how to say it without sounding vain or ridiculous, but I can’t stop seeing something wrong with my face. Especially around my mouth and jaw. It’s like there’s this droop on one side, and unevenness, and once I notice it I can’t unsee it.

It shows up in every photo, every reflection—windows, mirrors, even my phone screen when it goes dark. I’ll be trying to focus on work or getting ready to meet someone, and then I catch my face from a certain angle and it’s just… obvious to me. Like my mouth is sagging or my jawline is off. Other people say I look fine, or they say they don’t know what I’m talking about, but that almost makes it worse because I feel like they’re either being polite or they just aren’t looking closely enough.

And it’s started affecting my work. I’m an architect, so I have to present designs and meet with clients, and lately I’ve been avoiding presentations or trying to get out of client-facing things because I’m so aware of my face the whole time. I’m sitting there thinking they must be noticing it instead of listening to me. It’s become… it’s just taking over more than I want to admit.
Have you noticed that your mood has been affected when you focus on this issue with your face—like feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in things you usually enjoy?

I… I’m not sure how to answer that exactly. I mean, when I’m focused on it, I definitely don’t feel good, but I don’t know if I’d call it “hopeless” in the way you mean. It’s more like I get caught in this loop of looking and checking and thinking, “Why does it look like that?” and then I feel embarrassed and frustrated with myself for caring so much.

As far as losing interest in things… I don’t know. I haven’t really thought about it that way. It’s hard to separate what’s my mood and what’s just me being preoccupied with my face, if that makes sense. I wouldn’t want to say yes to something if I’m not sure. It’s just that when I notice it, it kind of colors everything for a while.
Do you find yourself having repeated, unwanted thoughts about your face that you can’t seem to get rid of, even if you try not to think about it?

Yes. Very much. It’s not like I’m choosing to think about it, exactly—it just kind of barges in. I’ll be doing something completely normal, like looking at a drawing or getting ready for a meeting, and then I’ll catch my reflection in my laptop screen or a window, or I’ll see a photo of myself, and suddenly all I can see is that droop around my mouth and the unevenness in my jaw.

And then even if I try to tell myself, “Stop, you’ve already looked, people say you look fine,” it doesn’t really settle. It feels so obvious to me. I keep replaying it in my head, like picturing how my face must look from the side or under office lighting, or wondering if it was visible when I was talking to someone. It’s intrusive, I guess—unwanted, definitely—but it also feels hard to ignore because it seems real when I see it.

That’s part of why I’ve started avoiding presentations or client meetings. I know that sounds extreme, but when I’m in front of people, I can’t just focus on the work. I’m thinking, “They’re looking at my mouth, they can see the sagging, they can tell one side is off.” Even when someone reassures me, I don’t really believe it. It’s like they’re being kind, or they don’t notice details the way I do.
Do you find yourself doing anything repeatedly—like checking your face in mirrors, taking a lot of selfies, or trying to cover or adjust your face—to deal with these concerns about your appearance?

Yes… I do. More than I probably want to admit.

Before work, especially if I know I have to see people, I can get stuck in the bathroom for ages checking the mirror. Not just a quick look—like, turning my head slightly, then looking straight on, then lifting my chin, then trying different lighting because I think maybe it’s the light, but then another angle makes it look worse. And then I’ll take pictures on my phone from different sides, because sometimes I don’t trust the mirror, but then the pictures make me panic more.

If there’s a family event, it can be even worse because I know people will take photos. I’ll redo my makeup, then undo it, then try again to make that side of my mouth look less droopy. I fuss with scarves too—like if I can arrange one near my jaw or neck in a way that distracts from it. It sounds ridiculous saying it out loud, but I can spend hours doing that before leaving the house.

And I ask my husband. I’ll say, “Does my face look lopsided today?” or “Can you see this side sagging?” He’ll say no, or he’ll say I look fine, but I keep asking because I don’t believe it. Then sometimes I compare myself to other women online, scrolling through photos and looking at their jawlines or mouths, trying to figure out if mine looks as bad as I think it does next to theirs. It’s exhausting, honestly, but I still do it.

Do you believe that the issue with your face — the droop around your mouth and uneven jaw — is something that others would notice as clearly as you do, or do you think it’s something that’s barely noticeable to them?

I know, rationally, that maybe other people don’t see it the way I do, because they keep telling me I look fine. My husband says it, people don’t react the way I imagine they will, and no one has actually pointed at my face or anything like that.

But it doesn’t feel barely noticeable to me. It feels… obvious. Like once I see the droop around my mouth or the unevenness in my jaw, I can’t unsee it, and then I assume everyone else must be seeing it too, especially in photos or if I catch my reflection in harsh lighting. It’s like my eyes go straight to it, and I imagine theirs do too.

That’s honestly why I’m here. I can’t stop seeing it in every photo and every reflection, and even when someone reassures me, it doesn’t really land. It still feels like this glaring thing on my face. I’ve started avoiding presentations and client meetings because I’m so convinced people will notice it when I’m talking. I know that might sound out of proportion, but in the moment it feels so real.
Has this concern about the droop around your mouth and uneven jaw caused you to avoid social situations, change your routine, or interfere with your ability to function at work or home?

Yes. It’s… it’s really interfering now. It used to be something I could sort of contain to getting ready in the morning or avoiding being in photos, but lately it’s spilled into everything.

The worst example was a major client presentation I was supposed to give. I had worked on it for weeks, and it was important—really important for the project and for how people at work see me. But the morning of it, I looked in the mirror and I just couldn’t get past how my mouth looked, like that one side was hanging lower and my jaw looked uneven. I kept imagining standing at the front of the room, talking, and everyone watching my mouth move and noticing it. I tried to push through it, I really did, but I ended up cancelling at the last minute. I made an excuse, but the truth was I couldn’t face being seen.

And there have been networking events too, related to an award—things I should have gone to, things that would have mattered for my career. I’ve missed those because I couldn’t bear the idea of people taking photos or looking at me up close. It sounds so small when I say it’s about my face, but the consequences haven’t been small. My project deadlines have started slipping because I’m losing time and avoiding meetings. At home, family gatherings have become tense because I either don’t go, or I’m late, or I’m so preoccupied that I’m not really present.

So yes, it’s changed my routine, and it’s affecting work and my family. It feels like things are starting to fall apart around this.
When people tell you they don’t see the droop or unevenness in your face, do you believe they are telling the truth, or do you think they’re just trying not to hurt your feelings?

I want to believe they’re telling the truth, especially my husband, because I don’t think he’s trying to be cruel or anything. But honestly… most of the time it feels like they’re just being kind. Like they don’t want to make me feel worse, or they think if they say, “No, I don’t see it,” I’ll drop it.

The problem is I can’t stop seeing it. The droop around my mouth, the unevenness in my jaw—once I catch it in a photo or in a reflection, it’s all I can focus on. So when someone says they don’t notice it, there’s this part of me that thinks, how could you not? It feels so obvious to me. Especially if I’m talking or smiling, I imagine it’s the first thing people are looking at.

And that’s why it’s gotten so hard with work. Even if people reassure me, I still feel exposed, like in presentations or with clients they’ll be watching my face and noticing that one side looks wrong. So I guess… I don’t fully believe them. I think they may be trying not to hurt my feelings, even if they mean well.

Have you ever felt that your concern about your facial appearance was so intense or persistent that it interfered with your ability to focus on anything else, or made it hard to function normally in your daily life?

Yes. Very much. It’s not just a passing worry anymore, where I can look in the mirror, feel bad for a few minutes, and then get on with my day. It takes over. I’ll be trying to focus on work, and instead I’m thinking about how my mouth looks when I talk, whether the droop is obvious, whether my jaw looks uneven from a certain angle. It’s like it sits in the front of my mind and everything else has to fight for space behind it.

I mean, I cancelled a major client presentation at the last minute because I couldn’t face standing there being seen. That was not a small thing. I had prepared for it, people were depending on me, and still I couldn’t make myself go through with it. And I’ve been missing networking events connected to an award, which I know sounds ridiculous when I say it out loud because those are opportunities I should be grateful for, but the idea of people looking at me or photos being taken just feels unbearable.

And now it’s affecting basic functioning. My project deadlines are slipping because I lose time spiraling about this or avoiding situations where I’ll have to be visible. Even family gatherings have started to fall apart around it — I either don’t go, or I go and I’m so distracted and tense that I’m not really there. So yes, it’s persistent, and it absolutely makes it hard to function normally.

Have you ever felt so certain about the droop around your mouth or the unevenness in your jaw that you believed it must be visible to others, even if they couldn't see it or refused to acknowledge it?

Yes. I mean… yes, that’s exactly what happens. I can be looking at a photo or even just catch myself in a window or a mirror, and I’ll see this droop around my mouth, and then the unevenness in my jaw, and it feels completely obvious. Not subtle. Not something I’m imagining in that moment. It feels like anyone looking at me would have to see it.

And when people say they don’t see it, I don’t really know what to do with that, because to me it’s right there. I’ll think, maybe they’re just being polite, or maybe they don’t want to upset me, or maybe they’re not looking closely enough. But I can’t believe it’s invisible. I just can’t. It’s become the thing I notice first in every reflection, every photo, every time I’m about to speak to someone.

That’s why presentations and clients have become so hard. I keep imagining them watching my mouth while I talk, noticing that it doesn’t look right, that my jaw is uneven. Even if nobody says anything, I feel like they must be seeing it and just not acknowledging it. So yes, I do feel certain about it a lot of the time, even when other people tell me I look fine.

So yes, it’s persistent, and it absolutely makes it hard to function normally.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has experienced any delusional beliefs regarding their facial appearance, which would help distinguish Body Dysmorphic Disorder (F45.22) from Major Depressive Disorder (F32.2) and Recurrent Depressive Disorder (F33.2).
doctor.question: Have you ever felt so certain about the droop around your mouth or the unevenness in your jaw that you believed it must be visible to others, even if they couldn't see it or refused to acknowledge it?

target_item.name: Preoccupation_with_Appearance
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because I can’t stop seeing this droop and unevenness around my mouth and jaw in every photo and reflection, and even when people tell me I look fine, it feels so obvious that I’ve started avoiding presentations and clients.
target_item.reason: The question is about the patient’s conviction that the perceived droop and jaw unevenness are visible to others despite reassurance, which directly relates to preoccupation with perceived appearance flaws.

patient.answer:
Yes. I mean… yes, that’s exactly what happens. I can be looking at a photo or even just catch myself in a window or a mirror, and I’ll see this droop around my mouth, and then the unevenness in my jaw, and it feels completely obvious. Not subtle. Not something I’m imagining in that moment. It feels like anyone looking at me would have to see it.

And when people say they don’t see it, I don’t really know what to do with that, because to me it’s right there. I’ll think, maybe they’re just being polite, or maybe they don’t want to upset me, or maybe they’re not looking closely enough. But I can’t believe it’s invisible. I just can’t. It’s become the thing I notice first in every reflection, every photo, every time I’m about to speak to someone.

That’s why presentations and clients have become so hard. I keep imagining them watching my mouth while I talk, noticing that it doesn’t look right, that my jaw is uneven. Even if nobody says anything, I feel like they must be seeing it and just not acknowledging it. So yes, I do feel certain about it a lot of the time, even when other people tell me I look fine.

inference.note: The patient's concern about a perceived facial deformity (droop around the mouth and uneven jaw) that is not observable to others, along with repetitive behaviors (mirror checking, photo taking, reassurance seeking), significant distress, and functional impairment (avoidance of work presentations, social situations, family events), strongly supports the diagnosis of Body Dysmorphic Disorder (F45.22). The patient's lack of insight (believing the defect is obvious to others despite reassurance) further aligns with this diagnosis. Major Depressive Disorder (F32.2) and Recurrent Major Depressive Disorder (F33.2) have been ruled out as the mood symptoms described are primarily tied to the preoccupation with appearance rather than a primary depressive syndrome.
